title_en: BVfK criticizes new e-car subsidy, calls for “effective concepts”
text_en: BVfK criticizes new e-car subsidy, calls for “effective concepts” The Federal Association of Independent Car Dealers (BVfK), which by its own account has more than 1,000 members, comments on the federal government's plans to introduce a purchase premium for electric cars and plug-in hybrids again next year. CDU/CSU and SPD have announced a premium for the purchase and leasing of new electric cars and plug-in hybrids. The subsidy of at least 3,000 euros is aimed at “households with low and middle incomes”. The upper income limit is 80,000 euros. Households with a monthly net income below 3,000 euros receive an additional grant of 1,000 euros. If there are children in the household, there is even more money. The maximum state subsidy for an e-car purchase is 5,000 euros. The BVfK supports the political goal of promoting low-emission mobility and securing jobs in the automotive industry. At the same time, the association warns of perverse incentives like those that earlier short-term subsidy programs already triggered. “Subsidies often only create flashes in the pan and lead to massive market distortions,” says BVfK President Ansgar Klein. “Not only the 2009 scrappage bonus has shown that artificially created demand peaks are followed by slumps – without any sustainable additional sales.” The association sees a central risk in renewed one-sided subsidization of new vehicles. It reduces innovation pressure on manufacturers and leads to rising prices and considerable depreciation for consumers. To relieve especially households with smaller incomes, the BVfK therefore calls for introducing a subsidy for used electric cars: 50 percent of the new-car premium for vehicles up to 3 years old / 50,000 km, and 30 percent of the new-car premium for vehicles up to 5 years old / 80,000 km. Only in this way could electric mobility truly reach the broad public, the BVfK says. “The environment does not benefit either if subsidized electric vehicles end up as used cars on scrap heaps and do not replace combustion engines in the further trading stage.” The BVfK also criticizes the earlier practice of treating EU new vehicles as used vehicles under subsidy law because of day registrations. This has massively disadvantaged both consumers and the EU new-car trade, which is important for competition. The association therefore demands a clear equal treatment of EU new vehicles, as the European legal framework also provides. “We need a funding model that equally takes into account the environment, market mechanisms and social justice,” emphasizes Götz Knoop, policy department at the BVfK. Short-term measures must not again benefit only the manufacturers. “Far more people work in the motor vehicle trade beyond the factory gates than in the factories themselves. A funding program must not lead to collateral damage, among others for independent trade.”

title_en: Who owns El Mayor, the restaurant where AMLO celebrated Claudia Sheinbaum?
text_en: Who owns El Mayor, the restaurant where AMLO celebrated Claudia Sheinbaum? Besides San Ángel Inn, Hunan or El Cardenal, there is another very popular venue among Mexican politicians: the restaurant El Mayor, a place that Andrés Manuel López Obrador even chose for a very special occasion. Well, it was in this place that the former president met with President Claudia Sheinbaum to hand over the ‘bastón de mando’ of the Fourth Transformation, a symbolic act with which AMLO closed his cycle in Morena. A dinner also attended by ‘las corcholatas’, where names such as Adán Augusto López, Ricardo Monreal, Manuel Velasco and Gerardo Fernández Noroña stood out, who enjoyed dishes of Mexican cuisine. Well, this is one of the restaurant's greatest attractions: the traditional food that can be enjoyed with one of the best views of downtown Mexico City, all of it the owner's idea. Who is the owner of the restaurant El Mayor? The woman behind El Mayor is chef Begoña Pérez Porrúa Suárez, who developed a great love for cooking after watching her grandmother prepare food since she was a girl. “I always liked it since I was little, I liked cooking, my grandmother is Basque, from Navarre, and she cooked all day, I loved getting into the kitchen,” said chef Begoña Pérez Porrúa in a conversation with RFI Español. Before fully devoting herself to gastronomy, Begoña completed a degree in Business Administration at the Universidad Iberoamericana and then traveled to Europe to learn about French cuisine. The chef began with a specialization at the Ritz Escoffier school, one of the most prestigious in the field, where she learned from the best chefs and acquired great discipline in the kitchen. “At the Ritz you had to learn the recipes from scratch, and it was work and more work, but the result was impressive. In the end, the preparation and decoration of the dishes was very meticulous. Presentation is important,” she added in the conversation about what she learned. From cafés to the restaurant where Sheinbaum and AMLO dined: When did El Mayor open? When her stay ended, in the early 2000s, she returned to Mexico to keep learning about gastronomy, and after two years the chef combined her knowledge of cooking and administration to start her own business: a café. But everything changed when the decision was made to renovate the building in which the first branch of Porrúa, her family's bookstore, had opened, since she saw the opportunity to realize her dream: opening a proper restaurant. Chef Begoña Pérez Porrúa proposed the idea, but her loved ones were not convinced of the business's potential: “Everyone saw it with fear, with uncertainty, as if they couldn't see that it would work.” Her relatives acknowledged that Begoña had great passion for gastronomy, but that she needed people to come and eat in order to succeed, since

title_en: “One Battle After Another” wins Oscar for Best Picture
text_en: “One Battle After Another” wins Oscar for Best Picture The 98th Academy Awards ceremony came to an end in Los Angeles. The statuette for Best Picture went to Paul Thomas Anderson's film “One Battle After Another”. The film was nominated in thirteen categories and won in six of them. Photo: Mike Blake / Reuters “One Battle After Another” also won awards for: - best director; - best supporting actor (Sean Penn); - best adapted screenplay; - best film editing (Andy Jurgensen); - best casting. The film “Sinners” received a record 16 nominations. It won four of them, including Michael B. Jordan's award for best actor in a leading role. The best international film was “Sentimental Value” by director Joachim Trier. The best documentary was “Mr. Nobody Against Putin”, made by the Russian teacher Pavel Talankin together with director David Bronstein. The Russian short animated film “Three Sisters” by Konstantin Bronzit did not receive a statuette. The award went to the Canadian film “The Girl Who Cried Pearls”, created by Chris Lavis and Maciek Szczerbowski. The winners of the “Oscars 2026” in other categories are listed in the Kommersant article.

title_en: Experts gather in Rome for new frontiers in precision oncology
text_en: Experts gather in Rome for new frontiers in precision oncology A conference organized by the Osservatorio Sanità e Salute with the contribution of Aiom. “We need real alliances: school, family, training, prevention. These are the engines for reducing the demand for health,” said Francesco Vaia, Director General of Health Prevention at the Ministry of Health, who also praised pharmacological innovation while speaking at the conference “Oncology of the future: patient-centered”, promoted by the Osservatorio Sanità e Salute under the patronage of Aiom and Cittadinanzattiva. Coordinated by Stefano Vella, professor of Clinical Research Methodology at the University of Rome “Tor Vergata”, the event explored recent successes in oncology research, focusing on the new frontiers of precision oncology. From anticipating innovative treatments at early stages to considering the needs of specific populations, such as patients with metastatic disease, up to the most fragile and elderly patients. “Prevention comes first in the anthology centered on the patient,” continued Anna Lisa Mandorino of the general secretariat of Citaddinanzattiva. “An oncology that looks to the future is one that prevents the condition of disease. This is already possible now with the tools we have available, including screenings. In Scotland one type of cancer was eradicated precisely through the massive practice of prevention. Future-oriented oncology also looks at the increasingly broad possibility of living with an oncological condition, because the condition reaches a level of chronicity, or the hope for everyone that one can recover from an oncological condition.” Constant progress in medical technologies has opened new paths for understanding and managing tumors. The application of cutting-edge methodologies in early diagnosis and personalized treatments has given rise to an increasingly targeted and effective approach: from anticipating innovative treatments at early stages to considering the needs of specific populations, such as patients with metastatic disease, up to the most fragile and elderly patients. “There is a need for acceleration in the approval of drugs that represent a breakthrough in treatment -” added Mauro Biffoni of the Istituto Superiore di Sanità. We are working on molecular targets. We have had faster approval models and access to therapies that, with further deployment, can be refined in their application.” Every neoplasm is different, just as every patient is. “There are approaches that prepare for surgery and accompany the patient into the next phase - so said Paolo Bironzo of the University of Turin. Precision medicine sees breast cancer as the first major approach. There are new-generation markers able to delay or prevent recurrence." But monoclonal antibody therapies have also made great strides. “Known as the bullet that can eliminate the tumor in eleven years - explained Lucia Del Mastro, University of Genoa - they have made great strides in the fight against cancer. The reduction in mortality, especially for breast cancer, is an undeniable fact.” New therapies are also emerging for leukemia, lymphomas and myelomas. title_en: Ukrainian drone production scales up across Europe
text_en: Ukrainian drone production scales up across Europe In a discreet building near the Mildenhall air base in England, drone maker Ukrspecsystems is ready to start up its new production line, like other Ukrainian arms companies seeking to secure their supply chain and increase their volumes. Germany, Denmark and now the United Kingdom: several Ukrainian drone manufacturers have announced in recent months plans to open sites outside their country. Ukrspecsystems, a specialist in reconnaissance drones, chose Mildenhall, in Suffolk (eastern England), a few dozen meters from a British military base. 👉 Live news on Ukraine is here In the warehouse area where the company has settled, no sign indicates the presence of the site, which was inaugurated on February 25 by British Minister of the Armed Forces Luke Pollard with the Ukrainian ambassador to the United Kingdom and former commander-in-chief of the army, General Valerii Zaluzhnyi. Within a few weeks, about 200 reconnaissance (ISR) drones per month will be assembled, and up to 1,000 eventually, explains its director, Rory Chamberlain. Notably the “Shark” models, which cost several tens of thousands of euros. Chamberlain adds: If Ukraine has multiplied its drone production since 2022, with more than four million units produced in 2025, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky, the needs remain enormous. But production conditions can be difficult in Ukraine. First because of the constant threat of Russian strikes, but also because of a still significant dependence on components imported from China, the Snake Island Institute, a defense think tank headquartered in Kyiv, recently pointed out. To speed up the pace, Ukraine set up in autumn 2025 a mechanism to ease the embargo on arms exports, to allow the transfer of technologies to allied countries, which can thus host assembly lines, whose finished products must for now be re-imported into Ukraine. The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) explains, in its recent Military Balance 2026 report: “Controlled” exports of certain types of weapons “will increase the production of drones destined for the front. We will have the necessary funds,” the Ukrainian head of state argued in September 2025. In mid-February, the Danish government announced it was in discussions to host the Ukrainian drone maker Skyfall. The company Fire Point, for its part, began construction in December of a propellant plant in Denmark, a propulsion product for missiles and drones, which is due to start operating in the autumn. The aim is to strengthen “the security of both Denmark and Ukraine,” argued Danish Defense Minister Troels Lund Poulsen. Ukrainian manufacturers “bring their knowledge” to European countries that are less advanced in developing these drones, in particular in the constant adaptability and evolution of onboard technologies (AI, jamming, etc.), Rory Chamberlain agrees before adding: The IISS further emphasizes: Since late 2024, Finland's Summa Defense has created several joint ventures with Ukrainian partners to produce drones
